sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Abolition of East India Company**: The Act formally liquidated the commercial and administrative powers of the **East India Company**, transferring all its territories, revenues, and armed forces directly to the British Crown.
• **Introduction of Crown Rule**: India was to be governed directly in the name of the **British Monarch**, marking the beginning of direct imperial colonial rule lasting until 1947.
• **Liquidation of Dual Government**: The system of **Dual Government** established by Pitt's India Act 1858 (Board of Control and Court of Directors) was completely abolished, streamlining administrative control under a single British cabinet minister.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Creation of a new office in London—**Secretary of State for India**—backed by a 15-member advisory body called the **Council of India**.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Cabinet minister of the British Government resident in London; political head of Indian administration.
Exercised complete authority and control over the Indian administration through the Viceroy; accountable to the British Parliament.
Often tested in Prelims as the supreme authority in London controlling the purse and policy of India.
Direct representative of the British Crown in India; Lord Canning was the first Viceroy.
Combined supreme executive authority in India while remaining strictly subordinate to the Secretary of State in London.
Tricky distinction: Viceroy was the title used when acting as Crown representative, Governor-General when dealing with the executive council.
15-member advisory body based in London; 8 members appointed by the Crown, 7 elected by the Court of Directors.
Designed to advise the Secretary of State; however, SoS could override the Council in most non-financial matters.
Frequently featured in Prelims statements regarding whether the council had binding or merely advisory powers.

items.definition: A member of the British Cabinet holding ultimate power over Indian governance, finance, and policy formulation from London.
The new designation given to the Governor-General of India, acting as the direct viceregal representative of the British monarch.
A statutory advisory council of 15 members established in London to assist the Secretary of State for India, possessing veto power over financial expenditure.
Royal declaration read out by Lord Canning at Allahabad on November 1, 1858, promising non-interference in religious matters, equal protection of law, and honoring of treaties with princely states.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **London (Metropolitan Center)**: Ultimate locus of power housing the Secretary of State, India Office, and the Council of India.
• **Calcutta (Administrative Hub)**: Seat of the Viceroy and the central executive machinery governing British provinces.
• **Princely States**: Reassured via the Queen's Proclamation, ending the doctrine of lapse and recognizing adoption rights to secure local loyalties.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Bureaucratic centralization in London, lack of representation for Indians in legislative bodies, and absolute veto power resting with British officials.
• **Policy Interventions**: Shift toward consultative administration, reorganization of the Indian Army, and the promise of gradual inclusion under subsequent Indian Councils Acts (1861, 1892).

items.title: Mnemonic for 1858 Act Structural Changes
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'S-V-C' (Stop Company Rule, Viceroy Created)
• **Decoded Meaning**: **S**ecretary of State created in London, **V**iceroy designated in India, **C**ompany rule completely abolished.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly prevents confusion between Company-era structures and Crown-era reforms.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Remember 'London Controls, Calcutta Executes'—the financial and policy purse strings remained firmly in the UK via the Secretary of State.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that the 15-member Council of India in London had absolute binding powers over the Secretary of State. This is incorrect; the Secretary of State could override the Council in most matters except those involving Indian revenues and expenditures.

Mains Value Addition: Analyze the Government of India Act 1858 as a watershed moment that marked the transition from 'merchant imperialism' to 'state imperialism', fundamentally altering how Indian grievances were channeled and suppressed.

keyTakeaways: The Government of India Act 1858 ended East India Company rule and established direct British Crown administration over India.
It created the powerful office of the Secretary of State for India in London, supported by a 15-member Council of India.
The Governor-General of India was given the additional title of Viceroy, serving as the Crown's direct representative in India.
